facts.query: How fast can bacteria multiply in food left out?
facts.explanation: In warm conditions many food bacteria divide in two again and again. Because each doubling builds on the last, a single cell can become millions within a working day, which is why food safety agencies warn about leaving food in the danger zone.

facts.sourceNote: Illustrative starting point

facts.label: Growth per doubling
facts.sourceNote: Each bacterial cell divides into two

facts.label: Doublings in 8 hours at one every 20 minutes
facts.sourceNote: Calculated from USDA FSIS 'Danger Zone' guidance: bacteria can double in as little as 20 minutes

plan.title: One bacterium left out on the counter
plan.caption: Best-case growth in the danger zone; real growth slows as conditions change.

facts.query: How much water does it take to produce our food?

facts.query: How much has overweight and obesity increased worldwide?

facts.query: Where were staple crops first domesticated?
facts.explanation: Farming began independently in several parts of the world. Wheat came from the Fertile Crescent, rice from China's Yangtze valley, maize from southern Mexico and potatoes from the Andes, while bananas, cassava, sorghum and cacao were tamed in other regions.

facts.label: Asian rice: lower Yangtze valley, China
facts.sourceNote: Fuller et al. (2009), Science; region approximate

facts.label: Maize: Balsas River valley, Mexico
facts.sourceNote: Matsuoka et al. (2002), PNAS; Piperno et al. (2009), PNAS

facts.label: Potato: Andes near Lake Titicaca, Peru
facts.sourceNote: Spooner et al. (2005), PNAS; region approximate

facts.label: Banana: Kuk Swamp, New Guinea highlands
facts.sourceNote: Denham et al. (2003), Science

facts.label: Cassava: southwestern Amazon, Brazil
facts.sourceNote: Olsen and Schaal (1999), PNAS; region approximate

facts.label: Sorghum: eastern Sudan
facts.sourceNote: Winchell et al. (2017), Current Anthropology; region approximate

facts.label: Cacao: upper Amazon, southeast Ecuador
facts.sourceNote: Zarrillo et al. (2018), Nature Ecology & Evolution

facts.explanation: Digestion breaks food into nutrients small enough to pass into the blood. It starts with chewing and saliva, continues with acid in the stomach and enzymes in the small intestine, and ends with the large intestine absorbing water.

facts.label: Mouth
facts.title: Mouth
facts.description: Teeth break food into pieces and saliva begins breaking down starches.
facts.sourceNote: NIH NIDDK: Your Digestive System and How It Works

facts.label: Oesophagus
facts.title: Oesophagus
facts.description: Swallowed food is pushed down to the stomach by waves of muscle contractions.
facts.sourceNote: NIH NIDDK: Your Digestive System and How It Works

facts.label: Stomach
facts.title: Stomach
facts.description: Muscles mix food with acid and enzymes that start breaking down proteins.
facts.sourceNote: NIH NIDDK: Your Digestive System and How It Works

facts.label: Small intestine
facts.title: Small intestine
facts.description: Bile and pancreatic enzymes finish digestion, and nutrients are absorbed into the blood.
facts.sourceNote: NIH NIDDK: Your Digestive System and How It Works

facts.label: Large intestine
facts.title: Large intestine
facts.description: Water is absorbed and gut bacteria break down some leftover fibre.
facts.sourceNote: NIH NIDDK: Your Digestive System and How It Works

facts.label: Rectum
facts.title: Rectum
facts.description: What remains is stored as stool until it leaves the body.
facts.sourceNote: NIH NIDDK: Your Digestive System and How It Works
